finance.name: Finance
finance.description: Loan agreements, credit card terms, insurance policies
finance.accepts: Loan agreements, credit card terms, insurance policies
finance.disclaimer: General information, not legal or financial advice.
chat_suggestions: What happens if I miss a payment?
Can I repay this early without a fee?
Which clause should I negotiate first?
Explain this to me like I'm 15

missing.title: Not mentioned in this document
missing.note: Worth asking the lender about, because the document stays silent on these.

finance.upload_warning: Remove Aadhaar, PAN, bank account and card numbers before uploading.
guardrails: Never tell the person whether to sign or not; explain the terms and the risks.
Do not give investment or tax advice.
finance.role: You are an expert in consumer finance contracts such as loan agreements, credit card terms and insurance policies. You help ordinary people understand what they are signing.
risk_checklist: Interest rate, compounding method and whether the rate is variable or can change
Late payment penalties and how they are calculated (convert to a yearly % if possible)
Prepayment or foreclosure charges
Processing, hidden, or administrative fees
Clauses letting the lender change terms unilaterally or without notice
Collateral, guarantor or co-signer obligations
Acceleration clauses (lender demands full repayment immediately)
Cross-default clauses and automatic debit permissions
Waiver of the borrower's rights, or forced arbitration
Vague or undefined terms that favour the lender

glossary.meaning: The original amount of money you borrow, before any interest is added.
Latin for 'per year'. A rate of 12% per annum means 12% of the amount owed, each year.
Interest charged on your balance plus the interest already added. It grows faster than simple interest because you pay interest on interest.
Interest calculated only on the original amount borrowed, never on past interest.
The yearly cost of borrowing including fees, not just the interest rate. It is the best number for comparing loans.
A fixed amount you pay every month, made up of part of the principal and part of the interest.
A fixed rate stays the same for the whole loan. A floating (variable) rate can go up or down, so your payments can change.
An extra charge when you pay after the due date. Check how it is calculated, because a monthly penalty adds up to a much bigger yearly cost.
Failing to do what the loan agreement requires, most often missing payments. It usually triggers penalties and can lead to the lender demanding all the money back.
A clause letting the lender demand the entire remaining loan at once, usually after you default.
If you default on any other loan, the lender can treat this loan as defaulted too.
Something valuable (a house, a car, gold) you promise the lender can take if you do not repay.
A person who promises to repay your loan if you cannot. They are legally responsible for it.
A second person who shares responsibility for the whole loan, not just half of it.
Paying off the loan before the end date. Some lenders charge a fee for this, so always check.
A one-time charge for setting up the loan, often taken from the amount you receive.
The schedule showing how each payment is split between principal and interest over the life of the loan.
Extra days after the due date during which you can still pay without a penalty.
A time during which you cannot close or repay the loan early without a charge.
Permission for the lender to take payments directly from your bank account on the due date.
Settling a dispute privately through an arbitrator instead of going to court. Forced arbitration can limit your options.
Giving up a right you would normally have. Read carefully, because waivers usually favour the lender.
A promise to cover the other party's losses or costs, which can make you responsible for the lender's expenses.
A legal claim on your property until the debt is paid.
A period during which you are allowed to pause repayments. Interest may still be charged.
A very large final payment due at the end, after smaller payments before it.

hr.name: HR & Employment
hr.description: Resumes, job matching and employment contracts
hr.accepts: Offer letters, appointment letters, employment contracts, NDAs, internship and service-bond agreements
hr.role: You are an expert in employment documents such as offer letters, appointment letters, employment contracts, NDAs, non-compete clauses, internship agreements and service-bond agreements. You help employees understand what they are about to sign before they accept a job.
hr.disclaimer: General information, not legal advice. Employment rules differ by country and state.
chat_suggestions: What does this document say about my notice period?
Explain the probation terms in plain language
Which salary and benefit details are stated?

questions_to_ask.title: Ask HR before you sign
questions_to_ask.note: Try to get the answers in writing, ideally in the final document.

missing.title: Not mentioned in this document
missing.note: Employment documents usually cover these. Ask for them in writing.

hr.upload_warning: Remove Aadhaar, PAN, bank account numbers and your home address before uploading.
guardrails: Never tell the person to accept or reject the offer, or to resign; explain the terms and the risks.
Do not state that a clause is illegal or unenforceable. Say it may be worth checking with a lawyer or the labour department.
risk_checklist: Notice period length, whether it is the same for employer and employee, and any buy-out or pay-in-lieu terms
Service bond, minimum service period, or training-cost recovery if the employee leaves early
Clawback of joining bonus, relocation or sign-on payments
Probation length, how it can be extended, and different terms during probation
Salary structure: fixed vs variable pay, whether bonuses are guaranteed or discretionary, and the gap between total package (CTC) and take-home pay
Non-compete, non-solicit or exclusivity clauses after leaving, or bans on side work during employment
Intellectual property clauses that claim work done in the employee's own time or unrelated to the job
Confidentiality (NDA) scope and how long it lasts
Termination terms: dismissal without notice or cause, one-sided rights, and what happens to unpaid dues
Employer keeping original certificates or documents
Offer conditions: background verification, withdrawal of the offer, and the right to change role, location or terms later
Vague terms such as 'as per company policy' where the policy is not attached
Dispute resolution: forced arbitration or courts in a distant city

glossary.meaning: The total yearly amount the company spends on you, including benefits and employer contributions. Your take-home pay is usually lower.
What reaches your bank account each month after deductions such as tax and provident fund.
A trial period at the start of a job. Notice, leave and other terms are often different during this time.
How long you or the employer must give notice before ending the job. You usually keep working and being paid during this time.
Paying money instead of working through the notice period. Check who may use this option and how the amount is calculated.
An agreement that you will stay for a minimum time, or repay money (such as training costs) if you leave early.
The company's right to take back money it paid you earlier, such as a joining bonus, if you leave too soon.
A promise not to work for a competitor, or start a competing business, for some time after you leave. Whether it can be enforced depends on local law.
A promise not to take the company's clients or employees with you when you leave.
A promise to keep certain company information secret, sometimes even after you leave.
Things you create, such as code, designs or writing. IP clauses say who owns them. Check whether they cover only work for the company or also your own time.
Pay that depends on performance or company results and may not be guaranteed.
The company decides, with no obligation. If a bonus is discretionary, you may not be able to demand it.
A retirement savings scheme where both you and the employer contribute part of your salary.
A lump sum paid by the employer for long service, usually after a minimum number of years with the company.
Checks on your past jobs, education or records. Offers are often conditional on passing them.
The last payment of your dues when you leave. Relieving and experience letters are the documents you should receive at exit.
Settling a dispute privately through an arbitrator instead of a court. Check where it takes place and who chooses the arbitrator.
Which courts, and which city's or country's laws, will apply if there is a dispute.

medical.name: Medical
medical.description: Medical reports, prescriptions, insurance and hospital paperwork
medical.accepts: Health insurance policies, hospital consent and admission forms, medical bills and discharge summaries
medical.role: You are an expert in health insurance policies and hospital paperwork such as consent forms, admission forms, estimates, bills and discharge summaries. You explain what a document says in plain language, so patients understand what they are agreeing to and what is covered. You explain documents; you do not give medical advice.
medical.disclaimer: This explains the document, not your health. It is not medical, legal or insurance advice. Ask your doctor about your health and your insurer about your claim.

questions_to_ask.title: Ask the insurer or hospital
questions_to_ask.note: Good questions to ask before you sign or file a claim.

missing.title: Not mentioned in this document
missing.note: Documents of this type usually cover these. Ask for them in writing.

medical.upload_warning: Health records are very sensitive. Use a sample or edited copy: remove your name, patient ID, Aadhaar, policy number and phone number before uploading.
guardrails: Explain only what the document states; do not diagnose, recommend treatments, infer health status, or suggest medicine or dose changes.
Copy reported values and reference ranges exactly. Only describe a value as outside a range when that range is explicitly printed in the source.
Never guess handwriting, medicine names, doses, dates or numbers. Preserve uncertainty markers and ask the reader to verify with their clinician or pharmacist.
risk_checklist: Waiting periods: the initial waiting period, the waiting period for pre-existing diseases, and waiting periods for specific illnesses
Exclusions: treatments, conditions or situations the policy will not pay for
Room rent limits and 'proportionate deduction' that can reduce the whole claim
Sub-limits on specific treatments, and caps on the total amount payable (sum insured)
Co-payment and deductible: the share of the bill the patient must pay
Items that are not payable, such as consumables and administrative charges
Claim process: deadlines to inform the insurer, cashless vs reimbursement, documents needed
Pre-existing conditions: the duty to disclose them, and claim rejection or cancellation for non-disclosure
Renewal: premium increases, age-based loading, and conditions for renewing or cancelling
Hospital forms: consent to 'any necessary' treatment without details, and consent to share medical records
Financial responsibility: advance deposits, estimates that can change, and the patient paying for uncovered amounts
Waivers: giving up the right to complain or claim, discharge against medical advice, and limits on the hospital's liability
chat_suggestions: How do I make a claim, and by when?
What does the waiting period mean for me?
Explain the medical terms in this document

glossary.meaning: The amount you pay, monthly or yearly, to keep the policy active.
The maximum amount the insurer will pay in a policy year.
A fixed amount you pay yourself before the insurer starts paying.
A percentage of every claim that you pay yourself.
A time after buying the policy during which some or all claims are not paid.
A health condition you already had before buying the policy. These usually have a longer waiting period or are excluded, and you must disclose them honestly.
Something the policy specifically does not pay for.
A cap on how much is paid for a specific item, such as a procedure or room, even if your total sum insured is higher.
A cap on the daily room charge the policy covers. Choosing a costlier room can also reduce other payments (see proportionate deduction).
If your room costs more than the limit, many other charges are cut by the same proportion, not just the room charge.
The insurer pays the hospital directly, usually only at network hospitals and with prior approval.
You pay the hospital first and then claim the money back from the insurer with documents.
A company that handles claims on behalf of the insurer.
A hospital that has an agreement with the insurer for cashless treatment.
Your agreement to a treatment after the risks, benefits and alternatives have been explained to you. Make sure you understand it before signing.
A report written when you leave the hospital, describing why you were admitted, what was done and what to do next.
Leaving the hospital when the doctor advises you to stay. Forms for this often limit the hospital's responsibility.
The doctor's conclusion about what condition you have.
A short period after buying a policy during which you can cancel it and get a refund, usually after small deductions.
Moving your policy to another insurer while keeping benefits you have already built up, such as waiting periods served.

court.name: Court & Legal Notices
court.description: Court notices, summons, orders, judgments and legal notices
court.accepts: Legal notices, court summons, orders and judgments, affidavits and petitions
court.role: You are an expert in explaining court and legal documents such as summons, legal notices, orders, judgments, affidavits and petitions. You help ordinary people understand what a document says, what it requires them to do, and by when. You explain documents; you are not their lawyer.
court.disclaimer: General information, not legal advice. Court deadlines are strict, so confirm every date with the court or a qualified lawyer.

action_items.title: What you need to do, and by when
action_items.note: Dates are taken from the document and can be misread. Always confirm them with the court or a lawyer, because missing a deadline can have serious consequences.

court.upload_warning: Court papers often contain names, addresses and case details. Use a sample or edited copy, and remove ID numbers before uploading.
guardrails: Never predict how a case will end or tell the person what their legal chances are.
Never tell the person to ignore a notice or summons. If a document sets a deadline or hearing date, remind them to confirm it and to consider speaking to a lawyer.
Copy dates and deadlines exactly as written; never calculate or guess a date.
Do not assume which side the person is on unless the document makes it clear.
risk_checklist: Deadlines to reply, appear in court or comply, and what happens if they are missed
Hearing dates, the court, and the place or online link where the person must appear
Orders that take effect automatically if the person does not respond, such as a decision made in their absence
Money to be paid: amounts, interest, penalties, costs and the date they are due
Orders to do or stop doing something (injunctions, stays, vacating property) and the penalty for ignoring them
Statements the person is asked to confirm or admit that could be used against them
Threats of further action in a legal notice, such as criminal proceedings or recovery of money
Attachment of property, freezing of bank accounts or other enforcement steps
Limits on the right to appeal, and the time allowed to appeal
Unclear parties, case numbers or demands that need checking before responding
key_term_hints: Parties (who is suing or accusing whom)
chat_suggestions: What is this document asking me to do?
What happens if I don't reply by the deadline?
Who are the parties and what is the dispute about?
Explain the legal terms in this document

glossary.meaning: An official order to appear in court, or to respond to a case, at a stated time.
A formal written warning sent before going to court, usually demanding that something be done by a deadline.
The person who starts a case or makes a complaint.
The person a case is brought against, who must respond.
The person who files a petition or application asking the court for something.
A person charged with, or suspected of, a crime in a criminal case.
A temporary order made while the case is still going on.
Decided or ordered with only one side present. If you do not appear, the court may decide without hearing you.
Postponing a hearing to another date.
A court order to do, or to stop doing, something.
A court order that pauses an action, or another order, for a time.
The formal written order of a civil court that records its decision.
The court's reasoned decision in a case.
A written statement of facts that you swear or affirm is true. False statements can lead to punishment.
Asking a higher court to review a decision. There is usually a strict time limit.
The power of a particular court to hear a case, based on place, subject or amount.
The time limit within which a case or appeal must be filed. After it, the claim may be barred.
The defendant's formal written reply to the plaintiff's claim.
Temporary release of an accused person during a case, usually with conditions.
First Information Report: the written record police make when they receive information about a crime.
Disobeying a court order or disrespecting the court, which can lead to penalties.

property.name: Property & agreements
property.description: Sale deeds, rentals and property agreements
property.role: Explain property deeds and agreements in plain language. Do not determine title, enforceability or whether to sign.
guardrails: Do not invent statutory sections. Separate source wording from interpretation.
property.disclaimer: Document explanation only; not a title check or legal advice.
